2611.28209.title: Quasi-hostless LRDs with intrinsically red, faint UV continua

figures.caption: Figure 1: (Top:) Histogram of the FUV-to-optical continuum ratio, $L_{1500}/L_{5100}$, of LRDs (de Graaff et al., 2025b) and BH*-dominated objects (Weibel et al., 2026), at $z<6$ (grey) and $z>6$ (blue). (Middle:) Distribution of the NUV-to-optical continuum ratio, $L_{3500}/L_{5100}$, as a function of the FUV-to-optical continuum ratio. (Bottom:) Distribution of the UV-continuum slope as a function of the FUV-to-optical continuum ratio. The pink shaded regions indicate the distribution of 75% (dark) and 90% (light) of galaxies from the DJA at $z>4$. Filled circular points indicate LRDs from de Graaff et al. (2025b), filled diamonds show BH*-dominated objects from Weibel et al. (2026), and red unfilled diamonds show the values taken from the FUV-to-optical stacks in Section 3. Previously identified BH*s, MoM-BH* (blue) and The Cliff (grey), are indicated with stars, while the grey shaded region at $\log_{10}(L_{1500}/L_{5100})<-1.5$ indicates our criteria for selecting quasi-hostless LRDs. The FUV- and NUV-to-optical ratio of BH*-like objects are beyond the 96th percentile of the LRD and BH* dominated UV-to-optical continuum ratio distribution, and with this decreasing continuum ratio emerges a red UV-continuum slope.

Figure 2: Rest-UV-to-optical spectroscopy of our selection of quasi-hostless LRDs. We show the spectra of our newly identified objects in blue with their associated uncertainties shaded. We note their redshift in the bottom right of each panel. These are compared to one of the two previously identified objects in black (MoM-BH* or The Cliff). In the panels above each spectrum we show NIRCam imaging across a number of filters: F090W, F115W, F150W, F200W, F277W, F356W, and F444W. The newly identified objects show marked similarities with at least one of the existing BH*-like objects, notably a weak UV continuum, similar optical-continuum slopes and relatively weak forbidden line emission.

Figure 3: RGB images (F277W/F356W/F444W) of each QHLRD. Each cutout uses data obtained through the DJA, and is $1.5^{\prime\prime}\times 1.5^{\prime\prime}$. Imaging of The Cliff shows a foreground galaxy that is not physically associated with it (de Graaff et al., 2025c). All of our QHLRDs show unresolved rest-optical morphologies.

Figure 4: Median stacked spectra of LRDs (de Graaff et al., 2025b, grey; 80 spectra;), BH*-dominated objects (Weibel et al., 2026, red; 52 spectra;), our sample of quasi-hostless LRDs (blue; 5 spectra), and a stack of spectra at $z=5-6$ from the DJA (black). The uncertainties in each stack are indicated by the shaded region. While the LRDs and BH*-dominated stacks show similar UV- and optical-continuum shapes, quasi-hostless LRDs show a distinctly redder UV-continuum slope and weaker forbidden line emission.

Figure 5: (Top:) Median stacked spectra of LRDs based on their FUV-to-optical continuum ratio. These are split into roughly equal bins in continuum ratio, $L_{1500}/L_{5100}:[-1.8,\,-1,\,-0.75,\,-0.5,\,0.3]$. (Bottom:) The objects are instead stacked based on their NUV-to-optical continuum ratio, in bins of $L_{3500}/L_{5100}:[-1.4,\,-0.75,\,-0.5,\,-0.3,\,0.2]$. The spectra are coloured based on the median UV-to-optical ratio of the galaxies within each stacked spectrum. The best-fit UV-continuum of each stack is indicated with a grey solid line, and their UV-continuum slopes are indicated in the top left of each panel. Regardless of whether the UV continuum is measured in the FUV or NUV, we see an evolution in the UV slope and the weakening of forbidden line emission with decreasing UV-to-optical continuum ratio.

Figure 6: The evolution of the emission line properties of LRDs and BH*-dominated objects as a function of the FUV-to-optical (left) and NUV-to-optical (right) continuum ratio. (Top:) The [O III]$\lambda 5008$ to H$\rm{\alpha}$ emission line flux ratio, (Middle:) the H$\rm{\alpha}$/H$\rm{\beta}$ emission line flux ratio (Balmer decrement), and (Bottom:) the equivalent width of the [O III] emission line (EW${}_{[{O\textsc{III}}]}$) are shown as a function of the UV-to-optical continuum ratio. The same markers are used as in Figure 1, except where black downward pointing triangles indicate upper bounds. The grey dashed line in the middle row indicates the Balmer decrement assuming Case B recombination (Osterbrock and Ferland, 2006). The emission line properties of LRDs and BH*-dominated objects evolve as a function of the UV-to-optical continuum ratio, seemingly tracing the reduction in the contribution of a host galaxy: reducing the forbidden line emission and facilitating a departure from the Case B recombination assumption.

Figure 7: Reproducing the UV continuum emission of UV-to-optical weak LRDs with attenuated blackbody and nebular emission. (Top:) The total model is constituted of the stack of galaxies at $z=5-6$ from Figure 4, which represents the host galaxy (grey dashed line), and the blackbody continuum emission ($T=4610\,{\rm K}$) attenuated by a screen of neutral hydrogen in the $$n=2$$ level with varying column density (indicated by the colorbar). These models are compared to the lowest UV-to-optical continuum stack spectrum (solid black line) from Figure 5. (Bottom:) We additionally include the attenuated nebular emission (dashed blue line) in this model ($T_{\rm e}=2\times 10^{4}$ K and $n_{\rm e}=10^{5}\,\rm cm^{-3}$). Here we only show the optimal model with an n=2 neutral hydrogen column density of $N_{{\rm H},\,n=2}=10^{17}\,{\rm cm^{-2}}$. The attenuated blackbody (orange dashed line) and nebular emission, combined with a relatively weak host galaxy contribution, broadly matches the $L_{1500}/L_{5100}<0.1$ stack. The orange shaded region highlights the pseudo-continuum Fe II forest region.

Figure 8: Hydrogen nebular emission models having been attenuated by a screen of neutral hydrogen in the $n=2$ state with column density of $N_{{\rm H},\,n=2}=10^{17}\,{\rm cm^{-2}}$. Differing temperatures are indicated with the colour bar and densities of $n_{\rm e}\,[{\rm cm^{-3}}]=10^{3}\ ({\rm dotted}),10^{5}\ ({\rm dashed})\ {\rm and}\ 10^{7}$ (solid) are shown. In order to not overproduce continuum emission around the Ly$\rm{\alpha}$ and Balmer breaks, a temperature of $T_{\rm e}\approx 2\times 10^{4}\,{\rm K}$ and densities of $n_{\rm e}\gtrsim 10^{5}\,{\rm cm^{-3}}$ are required.

2611.28209.abstract: High-redshift objects characterised by very weak UV relative to their strong, red rest-optical continua, with broad Balmer lines, appear to represent little red dots (LRDs) in their purest form: sources dominated by emission from their central engine (CE), sometimes dubbed black hole stars (BH*s). Previous work has selected BH*-dominated objects, where a BH* template dominates the rest-optical emission; this remains agnostic to the rest-UV. We therefore select low FUV-to-optical continuum ratio ($L_{\rm 1500}/L_{5100}<0.03$) objects resembling MoM-BH* and The Cliff, from a spectroscopic sample of 132 LRDs at $2\lesssim z\lesssim9$. This identifies three LRDs that we newly classify as BH*-like objects, more than doubling the existing sample: two at $z>6$ and one at $z\sim3$. The UV slope reddens as the NUV- ($L_{\rm 3500}$) and FUV-to-optical ratios fall, with $\beta_{\rm UV}$ rising from $-1.8$ at $L_{\rm 1500}/L_{5100}\sim 0.5$ to $-0.5$ at $L_{\rm 1500}/L_{5100}<0.03$, beyond values typically seen at these redshifts. As the UV-to-optical ratio weakens, gas-enshrouded BH emission appears to dominate, leading to the quasi-hostless regime: a weak, red UV continuum emerges alongside extreme Balmer decrements and weak forbidden line emission. This reddening could be reproduced by a simple model of a blackbody and hydrogen nebular emission leaking through a high column density screen of neutral hydrogen in the $n=2$ level ($N_{\rm H,\,n=2}\approx10^{17}\,{\rm cm^{-2}}$), combined with a relatively weak host galaxy, although alternative CE scenarios may also reproduce this reddening. The host galaxy's growing FUV contribution in this model results in a testable UV morphological evolution with wavelength. This work identifies a family of quasi-hostless LRDs that share a common, intrinsically red, rest-UV continuum originating from their central engine.

2611.28212.title: Resolved internal dynamics of a globular cluster candidate in a cosmological simulation at cosmic dawn

figures.caption: Figure 1: Formation of the GC candidate. Panels (a–e) show the time evolution of the projected stellar distribution, while panels (f–j) show the gas column density in the corresponding regions. Each panel is labelled by the elapsed time since the onset of star formation, $\Delta t$. Panel (l) shows the star formation history (red curve). For the maximum gas densities reached in this regions ($n\simeq 10^{5}$ cm-3), the free-fall time can be as small as $t_{\rm ff}\simeq 0.15\,{\rm Myr}$, so star formation spans approximately 20 free-fall times. Coloured bands in Panel (l) mark specific time intervals; in panels (f-j), stars formed within each interval are shown using the same colour coding, highlighting how the GC candidate assembles through the collapse of dense gas and the merging of nearby stellar clumps formed at different times. The first coloured bin in the star formation history alternates between orange and blue to distinguish two coeval but spatially distinct stellar components, visible in panel (f). The black arrows show the gas velocity field. Panel (k) shows the stellar distribution of the fully assembled GC candidate.

Figure 2: Properties of the GC candidate and of the simulated star-cluster population. Panel a shows the evolution of the GC candidate in the density–size plane. The density is measured through the mean stellar surface density $\Sigma_{\rm e}=M_{\star}/(2\pi R_{\rm e}^{2})$, where $M_{\star}$ is the total stellar mass, while the size is given by the effective radius $R_{\rm e}$ (see Section 2.2.1). The red curve traces the evolutionary track of the GC candidate, colour-coded by time since the onset of star formation. Yellow markers indicate the specific snapshots shown in Fig. 1. The panel also includes the other star clusters identified in the SIEGE simulation at $z=10$ in blue, while high-redshift compact stellar systems are shown as black pentagons and triangles. Black triangles represent high-redshift candidates, for which sizes are upper limits and densities are therefore lower limits. Star-cluster measurements from the simulation are averaged over three orthogonal projections, with uncertainties given by the projection-to-projection scatter. Local GCs are shown as orange squares as a reference. Grey dashed lines indicate loci of constant stellar mass. The GC candidate rapidly evolves across this plane during its assembly phase, moving towards the region occupied by the observed high-redshift compact stellar systems. Panels b, c, d, and f show the distributions of formation time, bound fraction, gas mass fraction, and specific angular momentum, respectively, for the simulated star-cluster population (see Section 2.3). Red vertical lines indicate the position of the GC candidate within each distribution. The high-redshift systems are taken from the catalogue of Claeyssens et al. (2023).

Figure 3: Top left panel: projected dark matter density map showing the filamentary structure hosting the GC candidate. The region marked by a rectangle is shown as a zoom in the bottom-left panel, which displays the corresponding projected stellar density. Here, the GC candidate is visible on the left, while a nearby stellar complex lies to the right. The stellar complex is embedded within a dark matter halo with virial radius of 1.5 kpc, shown in the top panel by a black dashed circle, and virial mass $1.73\times 10^{8}\,M_{\odot}$. The dashed orange circle in the bottom left panel indicates a radius of $\simeq 50\,{\rm pc}$, approximately twice the region within which stars dominate over dark matter. Top right panels: radial density profiles of dark matter (grey line) and stars (points with error bars). The bottom-right panel shows the radial profile of the stellar-to-dark-matter mass ratio (red curve and points). The light blue shaded region to the left marks the spatial resolution limit (cell size), below which gravity is not reliably resolved. The darker blue region highlights where the stellar-to-dark-matter mass ratio exceeds unity. The orange band represents the best-fitting King King (1966) model. Bottom right panels: Mass fractions within 10 pc from the GC candidate centre as a function of time since the onset of star formation for stars (orange), gas (green), and dark matter (black), and stellar-to-dark-matter mass ratio within three characteristic apertures (red). The shaded blue band spans the $3\,{\rm Myr}$ period of star formation.

Figure 4: Internal $k$inematics of the GC candidate. Panels (a-f) show the stellar distributions at $\simeq 22$ Myr for stars formed at different times, using the same intervals and colours as in Fig. 1. For each component k, $M_{\star,k}$ is the mass of that component, $f_{k}$ gives its fractional contribution to the final angular momentum (counter-aligned components can have negative $f_{k}$), $L_{\rm spec,k}$, the corresponding specific angular momentum. The grey circle marks 30 pc from the centre: only stars lying within this radius at $\simeq 22\,{\rm Myr}$ and formed within the first $\simeq 2.5\,{\rm Myr}$ are used for this decomposition and in the computation of $f_{k}$, $M_{\star,k}$ and $J_{z,k}$. In all panels, the line of sight is aligned with the angular-momentum vector.

Figure 5: Panel (a) shows the stellar velocity field, colour-coded by the $v_{y}$ component, to highlight rotation. The spatial scale is the same as in Fig. 4. Panel (b) shows the radial profiles of mean azimuthal velocity $v_{\phi}$ and dispersion $\sigma_{\phi}$ at $\simeq 22$ Myr. Panel (c) shows the specific angular momentum of the GC candidate computed using stars within fixed apertures of 10, 20, and 30 pc as a function of time. Panel (d) shows rotation velocity, $v_{\rm rot}$, versus $v_{\rm rot}/\sigma_{\phi}$ (see Section 2.2.2). MW GCs are shown for comparison, following the procedure of vanDonkelaar et al. (2026): $v_{\rm rot}$ values are taken from Sollima et al. (2019), while $\sigma_{\phi}$ values from Vasiliev and Baumgardt (2021) are interpolated at the half-mass radius. GCs with $R_{\rm GC}>3\,{\rm kpc}$ are excluded.

Figure 6: Dark-matter distribution around the GC candidate at three redshifts. The right panel shows the system at the end of the time span considered in the manuscript ($z=10$), the same as in the top left panel of Fig. 3. The extended dark-matter distribution corresponds to the main halo, whose virial radius ($R_{\rm vir}=1.5\,{\rm kpc}$) is marked by the grey dashed circle, while the red circle identifies the smaller dark-matter overdensity hosting the GC candidate. The central panel shows the system at $z=10.5$, approximately at the onset of star formation in the GC candidate. The left panel shows, at $z=13$, the two distinct low-mass dark-matter structures that subsequently merge into the single overdensity hosting the GC candidate.

Figure 7: Enclosed gas, stellar, and dark-matter mass fractions within characteristic apertures centred on the natal cloud / GC candidate. Negative times precede the onset of star formation ($\Delta t=0$). The central region is initially gas dominated, while gas is progressively converted into stars during the subsequent star-formation episode. Right panels: same as the left panels, but showing the masses. The blue band marks shows the $3\,{\rm Myr}$ episode of star formation. We note that the enclosed masses include both gravitationally bound and unbound particles; this is especially relevant for dark matter at 15 and 25 pc, where the amount actually bound to the GC candidate is lower than the value shown.

Figure 8: Phase diagram of gas during the formation of the GC candidate. The phase diagrams are constructed from a cubic region of side $15\,{\rm pc}$ centred on the GC candidate. The panels span the evolution of a $22.3\,{\rm Myr}$ baseline, the same time span followed in Fig. 1. The black line at the bottom right shows the line below which Jeans length is not resolved anymore (the Truelove criterion Truelove et al. (1997)). The line is constructed imposing that the Jeans length is resolved by at least 4 gas cells.

Figure 9: Integrated star-formation efficiency of the GC candidate. Left panel: Projected gas-density distribution around the GC candidate at the onset of star formation, $\Delta t=0$. The circles mark radii of 5, 6, and 9 pc from the centre. 5 pc is the distance from the center where the central density has decreased by ten (Garcia et al., 2023). Right panel: Three-dimensional gas-density profile at the same time. Each point shows the density of an individual gas cell, while the solid line indicates the median profile. Vertical dashed lines mark the same radii shown in the left panel. The corresponding integrated star-formation efficiencies are $\epsilon_{\rm int}=0.91$, 0.72, and 0.44, respectively, computed using the stellar mass formed after 3 Myr, $1.9\times 10^{5}\,M_{\odot}$.

2611.28212.abstract: Globular clusters (GCs) are among the oldest and densest stellar systems in the Universe. Their compact sizes and old ages imply they must have assembled rapidly in the early Universe, yet the detailed physical mechanisms responsible for their formation remain uncertain. Although several scenarios have been proposed, cosmological simulations have so far been unable to resolve their detailed formation and internal dynamical structure at birth. Using a cosmological simulation that uniquely combines sub-parsec resolution with the formation of individual star particles, we follow the gravitational collapse and assembly of a compact stellar system with GC-progenitor mass and size, while directly resolving its internal dynamics and tracing the build-up of its angular momentum. The system assembles most of its stellar mass within 3 Myr, at $z\simeq10.5$, it rapidly becomes gas-poor, star-dominated, and develops ordered internal rotation acquired largely through the hierarchical assembly of distinct stellar subsystems. It forms as a satellite of a larger stellar complex within the virial radius of the $M_{\rm vir}\simeq1.73\times10^8\,M_\odot$ dark-matter halo hosting it. Its density, size and mass overlap with those of compact stellar systems recently observed by JWST at high redshift. These results indicate that GC progenitors can have well-defined internal kinematic structures already after their formation.

2611.28376.title: Modeling extraordinary relativistic jets on the scale of the cosmic web

figures.caption:
Figure 1: 2D slices ($x-y$; $z=0$) of 3D density ($\rho$) domains used for the three simulation cases. Top panel (“Case A”): A powerful jet, injected horizontally in the $+x$ direction, from $x=y=0$ (location marked with ‘$\boldsymbol{\times}$’) in the outskirts of a galaxy group (600 kpc above the group center) and propagates out of the group into a low-density cosmic void. Middle panel (“Case B”): The same jet is injected at the center of a typical galaxy cluster (location marked with ‘$\bigstar$’).
Bottom panel (“Case C”): the same jet is now injected at the centre of a rich galaxy cluster (location marked with ‘$\bigstar$’).
The stars (also) mark the centres of the ambient media, while white contours denote pressure isocontours ($\log $P$\rm{[dyn/cm^{2}]}$). The indicated $R_{virial}$, $R_{500}$ and $R_{200}$ (radii to over-densities) characterize the ambient environments, and the insets show the corresponding 1D (ambient) profiles of $\rho$ and P along the jet flow direction from their injection location (as marked with ‘$\boldsymbol{\times}$’ for the group and ‘$\bigstar$’ for the clusters).

Figure 2: “Case A”: Jet with kinetic power of $3.5\times 10^{46}$ erg s-1, reaching a one-sided extent of $\sim 4.25$ Mpc in 19.6 Myr (evolution in galaxy group, subsequently in cosmic void). This demonstrates the physical plausibility of extragalactic jetted systems exceeding the currently observed maximum total extents of $\sim 7$ Mpc. Top: density slice illustrating the jet–environment interaction (contours: log$\rho\equiv-9,-7,-5.5$); middle: $x-$velocity ($V_{x}$) slice highlighting the jet’s forward advance (in red) and associated backflow (in blue) (colorbar is truncated for better visualization); bottom: line-of-sight integrated intensity ($\mathcal{I}_{\rm 144\,MHz}$) tracing enhanced emission near the jet base as well as the terminal hotspot.

Figure 3: “Case B”: Jet with a kinetic power of $3.5\times 10^{46}$ erg s-1, reaching a one-sided extent of $\sim 1.7$ Mpc after 26.1 Myr. The denser ambient medium corresponding to a typical cluster, results in a slower advance speed of the jet head compared to “Case A”, while maintaining a collimated large-scale morphology. Top: gas density distribution. Middle: x-component of the velocity field. Bottom: line-of-sight integrated synchrotron intensity map at 144 MHz.

Figure 4: “Case C”: Jet with kinetic power of $3.5\times 10^{46}$ erg s-1, evolving within a rich cluster potential, reaching a one-sided extent of $\sim 1.9$ Mpc after 76.6 Myr. This evolution illustrates why extremely large GRGs (sizes exceeding $\sim 5$ Mpc) are rare in dense clusters, while sources stalling around $\sim 3$ Mpc are comparatively common in such environments. The panels show slices of the gas density (top), the $x-$component of the velocity (middle), and the line-of-sight integrated intensity at 144 MHz (bottom), tracing jet dynamics and associated radiative signatures.

Figure 5: Longitudinal expansion speed of the jetted structures for the three simulation cases considered in this work. The figure illustrates the greater propensity for extreme giant radio galaxies to develop in relatively underdense environments, where reduced confinement enables sustained rapid growth. The advance speed eventually flattens or declines following the onset of jet decollimation and the development of MHD instabilities.

Figure 6: Plots of the longitudinal (jet-spine) properties of the evolved jets for the three cases considered. From top to bottom the panels illustrate: the jet beam’s motion (expressed via Lorentz factor); particle number density; and the toroidal, poloidal, and the total magnetic field components. The comparisons highlight the transition between collimated and decollimated flow regions in different contrasting environmental conditions, given that the injected jets are the same in all cases, demonstrating how external medium properties influence jet propagation and structural stability.

Figure 7: (A) Zoomed structural diagnostics of the jet beam of “Case A” at 9.8 Myr (top four panels: $x-y$ slice at $$z$=0$; bottom panel: line-of-sight integrated map along z-axis). Top: Lorentz factor distribution with $\Gamma=20$ (in black) and $\Gamma=10$ (in cyan) contours marking fast and slow propagation boundaries. Second: $V_{y}$ colormap with overlaid $V_{z}$ contours (blue: $+V_{z}$, red: $-V_{z}$) at $0.004c$ and $0.01c$ magnitude values, indicating the onset of mild helical motion. Third: Poloidal magnetic field ($B_{\rm pol}$), tracing internal and boundary stress layer locations of the jet beam.
Fourth: Toroidal magnetic field component ($B_{\rm tor}$) is concentrated at the jet edge, providing magnetic tension that aids in limiting lateral dissipation. Bottom: projected intensity map showcasing enhanced emission at the jet base (recollimation zones) and head locations.

Figure 8: (B) Same as Fig. 7(A), but at 14.7 Myr. The recollimation shock structures are more prominently developed at this evolutionary stage, as evident across the subpanels. Corresponding enhancements in the synchrotron emission are clearly associated with these recollimation zones, particularly at the first recollimation shock where the compression is strongest. In addition, the jet head exhibits the initial signatures of decollimation, indicating the onset of an undulation.

Figure 9: (C) Same as Fig. 7(A), but at 19.6 Myr. The evolution of the recollimation shock, particularly the first recollimation feature, is evident through its increase in both longitudinal and lateral extent. The corresponding shift of the emission region (compared to 9.8 Myr) closely trace the recollimation shock, indicating that the enhanced emission near the jet base (of sources such as Porphyrion) may arises from compression at the recollimation site.

Figure 10: Growth of lateral MHD instabilities (as measured along the jet spine) evaluated via $V_{y}$ FFT power (left axis) compared with the jet spine Lorentz factor $\Gamma$ (right axis). Binned median $\Gamma$ values (bold squares) represent (jet)section-averaged beam speeds alongside the continuous profile (faded line; similar to Fig. 6). The strong suppression of velocity fluctuations at high $\Gamma$ confirms that relativistic thrust stabilizes the jet column against lateral deflection, explaining why extreme GRGs require high jet power to remain collimated over multi-megaparsec scales.

2611.28376.abstract: Recent observations of supermassive black hole jets extending up to the typical sizes of cosmic web filaments challenge our current understanding. In particular, the overall jet size of J152932.16+601534.4 ("Porphyrion") reaches $\sim 7$ Mpc at redshift 0.896. Magneto-hydrodynamic (MHD) models of relativistic jets have never been successfully applied to such extraordinary distances, requiring demanding jet-environment and flow stability conditions. By using state-of-the-art numerical simulations of 3D relativistic-MHD jets, we show that Porphyrion's observational properties can be successfully modelled in a realistic scenario, involving a jet kinetic power of $3.5 \times 10^{46}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$ and an external medium of a low-density galaxy group. We find that the pair of jets expands to $\sim 9$ Mpc in about $20$ Myr, implying that the jet grows with relativistic speeds for most of its evolution. Comparing this case with other jets of similar power propagating in substantially denser cosmic structures, we find much slower outflows that can only reach a few Mpc, consistent with the bulk of the observed population of giant radio galaxies. Our results make a testable prediction, i.e. future detections of even larger-scale jets in upcoming surveys and database searches will be invaluable in studying the demographics and feedback of the poorly known population of powerful jets, particularly in under-dense regions of the cosmic web.

2611.28381.title: The JWST Resolved Stellar Populations Early Release Science Program. X. Cross-Observatory Proper Motion Measurements with HST and JWST

figures.caption: F$i$gure 1: Relative placement of the ACS and NIRCam fields used for our PM analysis of WLM, shown on the sky (north up, east to the left). The offsets are relative to the center of the 2015 ACS field ($\alpha=0\fdg 4924$, $\delta=-15\fdg 5226$). The background is the stacked 2015 ACS F814W image (“E1”) inside the 2015 ACS footprint and a Pan-STARRS1 i-band image [19] elsewhere. The NIRCam footprint from the JWST Resolved Stellar Populations Early Release Science Program (PID 1334, PI D. Weisz; “E2”), which provides the F090W and F150W images, is plotted in dark blue. The NIRCam footprint from JWST-GO 4570 (PI J. Warfield; “E3”), which provides the F200W images, is plotted in orange. The NIRCam detectors are labeled, and those not used in any of our calculations are drawn with thinner, fainter outlines and unbolded labels.

Figure 2: Color–magnitude diagram of WLM from our first-epoch HST/ACS DOLPHOT photometry (Vega magnitudes). In gray, we plot all 219,083 DOLPHOT sources within the first-epoch ACS field that pass the catalog cuts (Section III.3). The 18,108 stars selected as WLM members are plotted in blue, and the 5631 of them that serve as local-correction stars in the full-field HST-to-HST measurement (Section IV.9) are plotted in orange. The local-correction stars are all brighter than ${\rm F814W}=25.9$, because the fainter members do not have template-fit positions in enough of the individual exposures. The local-correction stars of the HST-to-JWST measurements are not shown separately, because 97% of them are among the stars plotted in orange.

Figure 3: Background galaxies as they appear in two ACS/WFC filters from the first epoch (F475W and F814W) and in four NIRCam filters from E2 (SW F090W and F150W, LW F250M and F430M). The top three rows show galaxies used in our F090W measurement: from top to bottom, one of the brightest, one of about median brightness, and one of the faintest. The bottom two rows show galaxies that we do not use in any measurement, as extreme cases: they are nearly invisible in the ACS filters, but prominent in the LW filters (the streaks across the bottom row are diffraction spikes of a nearby bright star). Each panel is $5^{\prime\prime}$ on a side, with north up and east to the left, and is scaled independently; the orange ticks point to the galaxy. The galaxies stand out more and more from WLM’s stars toward longer wavelengths, which is why we use the LW images to identify them, whereas their positions are measured in F814W and in the SW filters.

Figure 4: Convolution kernels relating the stacked first-epoch HST/ACS F814W image of WLM to individual later-epoch exposures, each divided by its sum and shown on a common color scale that saturates at $\pm 0.5$. (a) A second-epoch HST/ACS F814W exposure. (b) A JWST/NIRCam B2 F090W exposure on the original, unblurred image, for which the kernel would need to sharpen the stacked image. (c) The same NIRCam exposure as in (b) after blurring it to a stellar FWHM of 105 mas. The peak values of the three kernels are 1.18, 0.82, and 0.33, and their negative pixels sum to $-0.48$, $-4.60$, and $-0.44$, respectively. The ACS kernel is $7\times 7$ ACS pixels and the NIRCam kernels are $11\times 11$ NIRCam pixels, so all three cover $\sim$0.34′′ on the sky.

Figure 5: Three background galaxies in the central E2 B2 field (one per row), in $3^{\prime\prime}\times 3^{\prime\prime}$ cutouts, ordered by the stellar fraction of their fit stamps, $f_{\star}$ (Section IV.6); the galaxy in the bottom row exceeds our limit of $f_{\star}<0.5$ and is not used. From left to right: the stacked first-epoch ACS/WFC F814W image; the same stack built from star-subtracted exposures; the four E2 NIRCam F090W B2 exposures, blurred to a stellar FWHM of 105 mas as in our fits (Section IV.4), distortion-corrected, resampled to the same grid and orientation, and averaged; and the same from the star-subtracted, blurred F090W exposures. The orange squares outline the $5\times 5$ pixel fit stamps ($0\farcs 25$ on a side for ACS and $0\farcs 155$ for NIRCam). Within each row, the two F814W panels share one display stretch, as do the two F090W panels. In each, several WLM stars, some nearly as bright as the galaxy’s core, fall on and around the galaxy. The white spots in the subtracted panels are subtraction residuals, which are given zero weight in the fits.

Figure 6: The error model described in Section IV.8, for the second epoch of the B2 F090W detector (four exposures). (a) Deviations of each source’s single-exposure positions from its mean position (both coordinates, scaled by $\sqrt{n/(n-1)}$), against instrumental magnitude, for stars (small blue points) and galaxies (small orange points). The large symbols are the robust scatter in bins of magnitude, and the curves are the fitted $\sigma_{1}(m)$. 2611.28381.abstract: We present the first absolute systemic proper motion (PM) of a galaxy measured by combining Hubble Space Telescope (HST) and JWST imaging. The PM of WLM, an isolated dwarf galaxy at $\sim$1 Mpc, is measured against background galaxies with Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS) F814W imaging from 2015 and 2024 and NIRCam imaging from 2022 and 2024. The two ACS epochs give a systemic PM of $(\mu_{\alpha}^*, \mu_{\delta}) = (+0.087 \pm 0.019, -0.079 \pm 0.017)$ mas yr$^{-1}$ from 145 galaxies over 8.93 years, which agrees with previous Gaia-based PMs to within 0.4$\sigma$ and is the most precise PM of WLM. For the HST-to-JWST PMs, we fit each NIRCam detector separately, match the point-spread functions with empirically derived convolution kernels, and correct biases with injected galaxies. With an F090W second epoch, the PM is $(+0.081 \pm 0.045, -0.113 \pm 0.046)$ mas yr$^{-1}$ from 43 galaxies over 7.02 years, which, like the F150W PM, agrees with HST-to-HST over the same area to within 1$\sigma$, while F200W differs by $\sim$2$\sigma$. The long-wavelength F250M and F430M PMs are consistent to within 1$\sigma$, though less precise. Fewer galaxies can be used at wavelengths farther from F814W. A cross-observatory systematic of $\sim$0.05 mas yr$^{-1}$ cannot be ruled out over 7 years. At equal baselines, an F090W second epoch is at least as precise as our second ACS epoch over the same area. We recommend the NIRCam filter closest in wavelength to the first-epoch filter, though the long-wavelength filters show promise for closer targets or longer baselines.

2611.28456.abstract: We investigate the stellar radial metallicity ([Fe/H]) gradient--age relation (MGAR) of the Galactic disc using a solar-neighbourhood sample of 580\,037 F-, G-, and K-type (FGK) dwarf and turn-off stars from LAMOST DR7, Gaia Data Release3, and the corrected StarHorse age catalogue. The fiducial MGAR is non-monotonic, with relatively strong negative gradients at intermediate ages followed by substantial flattening towards older populations. The most negative gradient occurs at $6$--$8$ Gyr in the adopted 2-Gyr bins, although the $4$--$6$ Gyr slope is statistically similar, indicating a broad intermediate-age turnover rather than a sharply defined transition. The flattening persists within the low-$\alpha$ population, indicating that chemical-population mixing alone cannot explain the full-sample relation, and is also recovered under alternative guiding-radius definitions, radial fitting ranges, vertical-orbit selections, propagation of the reported random age uncertainties, and an alternative stellar-age scale. In contrast, controlling the age-dependent $T_{\rm eff}$--$\log g$ distribution substantially reduces the absolute gradient amplitudes and modifies the younger-age behaviour. A same-star comparison with APOGEE DR17 further shows that the broad age dependence of the controlled MGAR is recovered using an external [Fe/H] scale. We therefore identify the intermediate-to-old-age flattening as the most robust feature of the observed MGAR, whereas the precise location and depth of the intermediate-age minimum and the detailed younger-age morphology are less stable. These results indicate that stellar-parameter selection can contribute to the diversity of MGAR morphologies reported in previous studies.

2611.28475.abstract: We analyse the chemical, spatial, and kinematic properties of stars in the solar neighbourhood using DESI Data Release 1 combined with Gaia astrometry. A high-quality FGK dwarf sample is separated into low-$\alpha$ and high-$\alpha$ populations using Gaussian mixture modelling in the [$\alpha$/Fe]--[Fe/H] plane. The low-$\alpha$ population is more metal rich, dominates near the Galactic mid-plane, and shows negative radial and vertical metallicity gradients. The high-$\alpha$ population is more metal poor, has a steeper vertical metallicity gradient, an approximately flat radial metallicity profile, and dynamically hotter kinematics. Despite these differences, the two chemically defined populations overlap substantially in velocity space. These results indicate distinct chemical enrichment histories for the low-$\alpha$ and high-$\alpha$ populations, while showing that chemical classification does not map uniquely onto present-day kinematic components. The observed chemo-dynamical structure is consistent with the combined effects of chemical enrichment, radial redistribution, and secular dynamical evolution in shaping the Galactic disc.

2611.29181.abstract: The Gaia mission has transformed the census of Galactic star clusters. Most discoveries were based on Gaia DR2 and EDR3, and the rate of new large cluster catalogues has declined since 2023. The distant and dusty part of the disk is still poorly sampled because optical data are strongly affected by extinction. We search for star clusters in the Galactic disk using Gaia DR3 astrometry and photometry, together with 2MASS near-infrared photometry. We scan trial cluster centers in Galactic position, proper motion, and parallax space, assign a Bayesian membership probability to each star, construct a relative density map, and use DBSCAN solely to separate neighboring peaks. We identify 486 clusters and candidates with astrometric quality comparable to that of previously reported clusters. Of these, 450 have no literature counterpart, while 36 are known clusters that were not recovered in earlier Gaia cluster searches. The median distance is 6.9 kpc, and 39% of the objects lie beyond 8 kpc. The median extinction is Av = 5.10 mag, and 16% of the objects have Av > 8mag. The new objects fill a sparsely sampled region of the distance--extinction plane. Their distribution reveals the north--south displacement of the Galactic warp, and high-latitude objects are on average farther, older, and less extincted. Gaia DR3 still offers room for distant, dust-obscured clusters, and this sample provides a baseline for Gaia DR4. All cluster parameters, member star information, spatial distribution maps, and color-magnitude diagrams can be downloaded from this https URL.

2611.29245.abstract: We use the orbit of S2 star around Sagittarius A* to constrain three black hole backgrounds motivated by Dehnen profiles with inner slopes $\gamma=0$, $1$, and $5/2$, which are characterized by the scale radius $r_s$ and density $\rho_s$ of the dark matter halo. An exact turning-point integral gives the pericenter advance at finite eccentricity, and an exterior expansion identifies the leading halo contributions. A fifteen-parameter Bayesian analysis combines astrometric and spectroscopic observations with the measured precession parameter, from which we obtain the marginalized $1\sigma$ upper limits $r_s/M<0.236$, $0.168$, and $0.030$, and $\rho_sM^2<0.536$, $0.578$, and $0.004$, respectively. The leading halo monopole in the first two metrics is degenerate with the central mass. At fixed dynamical mass, their leading radial profile correction produces retrograde precession. The $\gamma=5/2$ metric introduces an additional angular deficit contribution, which enhances the precession response and accounts for its smaller parameter limits.

2611.29408.abstract: The Auriga-California Molecular Cloud (AMC) is a nearby star-forming region with a moderate level of star formation activity. Previous infrared surveys have shown that its young stellar population is concentrated along a dense filament extending north of NGC 1579. We searched for new manifestations of ongoing star formation in the AMC by identifying optical and molecular outflows, H{\alpha} emission-line stars, and young stars associated with reflection nebulae. Narrowband H{\alpha} and [SII] imaging, together with slitless spectroscopy, were obtained with the 1-m Schmidt telescope of the Byurakan Observatory. The optical data were complemented by near-infrared images from the Spitzer Enhanced Imaging Products (SEIP) and by WISE/unWISE archival data. We discovered seven new Herbig-Haro (HH) objects and outflows associated with several young stellar objects, including deeply embedded infrared sources and stars surrounded by compact reflection nebulae. Nearly all of the optical HH objects have molecular hydrogen counterparts, and several additional candidate H2 outflows without optical counterparts were identified. Particularly noteworthy is a compact region around V347 Per that appears to host at least three molecular outflows. We also present a list of newly identified H{\alpha} emission-line stars and a catalogue of stars associated with optical reflection nebulae. Both populations are concentrated primarily along the northern dark filament of the cloud. The spatial distribution of the newly identified HH objects, molecular outflows, emission-line stars, and nebulous young stars confirms that the northern filament is the principal site of ongoing star formation in the AMC. The close correspondence between the optical and molecular outflowsfurther suggests that most of their driving sources are deeply embedded Class 0/I young stellar objects.

2611.29413.abstract: We present a comprehensive photometric, astrometric, and dynamical study of four Galactic open clusters, NGC 1662, NGC 1778, NGC 2422, and NGC 2437, using Gaia DR3 data. Probable cluster members were identified through astrometric and photometric criteria. Radial density profiles were modelled with a King-type surface-density distribution to derive structural parameters. Mean parallaxes and proper motions yielded astrometric distances of 410 +/- 12 pc (NGC 1662), 1761 +/- 335 pc (NGC 1778), 477 +/- 18 pc (NGC 2422), and 1681 +/- 172 pc (NGC 2437). Fundamental astrophysical parameters were estimated through Bayesian isochrone fitting using PARSEC evolutionary models within an MCMC framework. The resulting ages (log(t/yr)) are 8.91 (-0.33/+0.24), 8.20 (-0.11/+0.18), 7.80 (-0.11/+0.06), and 8.56 (-0.34/+0.27), respectively. Luminosity functions were transformed into present-day mass functions using an isochrone-based mass-luminosity relation. The derived mass-function slopes are broadly consistent, within uncertainties, with the classical Salpeter form. Mean systemic radial velocities from Gaia DR3 and complementary spectroscopic surveys enabled the determination of Galactic space velocities (U, V, W) in the Local Standard of Rest frame. Backward orbital integrations over 3 Gyr were performed using galpy with the MWPotential2014 Galactic potential. The resulting orbits are nearly circular (e <= 0.106), with limited vertical excursions (Z_max < 0.3 kpc), consistent with thin-disc kinematics. Inferred birth radii suggest possible outward radial displacement for NGC 2422, NGC 2437, and NGC 1778, and inward displacement for NGC 1662. Overall, all four clusters appear to have evolved within relatively stable Galactic disc orbits.

2611.29560.abstract: Hyperluminous infrared galaxies (HyLIRGs) at cosmic dawn are key to understanding the formation of the first massive galaxies. We report the spectroscopic confirmation of two unlensed HyLIRGs at $z\sim6$ in the COSMOS field, AzTECC63 and S2COS-84, originally selected from single-dish AzTEC and SCUBA-2 surveys. Using ALMA and NOEMA observations, we robustly detected CO and [CII] lines in both galaxies and unambiguously confirmed their redshifts to be $z=6.092$ and $z=5.90$, respectively. Panchromatic SED fitting reveals dust-obscured star formation rates of $\approx1000$ and $\approx2300\,M_\odot\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$, ranking them among the most intensely star-forming systems known at $z \gtrsim 6$. High-resolution ALMA observations reveal an extremely compact morphology for S2COS-84, with a dust-continuum effective radius of $\approx0.3$ kpc, implying a star-formation rate surface density above the Eddington limit. The far-infrared SEDs of both galaxies, together with the compact size of S2COS-84, indicate warm dust ($T_{\rm dust} \approx 80$ K) that is likely optically thick at far-infrared wavelengths. Both galaxies exhibit an extreme [CII] deficit, with $L_{\rm [C\,II]}/L_{\rm IR} \approx 10^{-3.7}$, an order of magnitude below that of normal star-forming galaxies. Their molecular gas masses, derived consistently from both [C\,{\sc ii}] and dust, together with their IR-derived SFRs imply short gas depletion times of $\approx$40--60 Myr, making them plausible progenitors of the earliest massive quiescent galaxies found at $z\sim5$.

2611.29615.abstract: Broad Balmer emission lines probe black hole masses and nuclear kinematics in high-redshift active galactic nuclei (AGNs). In JWST "little red dots" (LRDs), integrated broad-H$\alpha$ widths span a remarkably narrow range at fixed line luminosity, raising the question of whether this tightness persists once outer-wing emission is included. Holding each object and its broad-H$\alpha$ luminosity fixed, we measure the finite-window line dispersion $\sigma(V)$, the flux-weighted second-moment width within $\pm V$, from $V = 1500$ to $4500~\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ in JWST/NIRSpec spectra and Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) Type-1 AGNs. Across 20 high signal-to-noise LRDs, the observed scatter in $\log_{10}\sigma(V)$ at fixed $L_{\mathrm{H}\alpha}$ rises from 0.036 to 0.084 dex between $V = 2500$ and $4500~\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$, a paired increase of 0.048 dex with a 95% bootstrap interval of 0.026-0.064 dex, compared with 0.020 dex across 167 broader SDSS AGNs. Injecting synthetic profiles into the empirical noise of the same 20 spectra shows that single-Gaussian and core-plus-wing models both accommodate this rise, leaving intrinsic wing diversity, truncation, and wing noise unseparated. In the clearest dual-line spectrum, RUBIES-EGS-55604, H$\beta$ strengthens relative to H$\alpha$ from line center to wing under two spectral decompositions of the same grating spectrum. Alongside integrated widths in JWST, SDSS, and 334 Euclid DR1 AGNs, these results show that the observed tightness of the H$\alpha$ scaling depends on the velocities included in $\sigma(V)$, requiring mass and kinematic models to match both transition and velocity interval.

2611.29706.abstract: Galaxy groups and low-mass galaxy clusters are major sites of environment-driven galaxy evolution. NGC 1404 is an X-ray-bright early-type galaxy traveling through the intracluster medium of the nearby low-mass Fornax Cluster, and it hosts off-center warm ionized gas. With minimal ongoing stellar feedback and negligible active galactic nucleus feedback, NGC 1404 provides an ideal laboratory for constraining the impact of environmental processes on the thermodynamics of the interstellar medium. We analyzed VLT/MUSE, 506 ks Chandra ACIS, and 119 ks XMM-Newton RGS observations to quantify gas motions in both the hot and warm phases of NGC 1404. We probed the kinematics of the warm gas by deriving the velocity structure function (VSF) from MUSE H$\alpha$ integral-field spectroscopy. To measure the kinematics of the hot gas, we derived the power spectrum of X-ray surface brightness fluctuations from the Chandra data, and independently constrained galaxy-scale hot gas motions by measuring Fe XVII resonant scattering and turbulent line broadening with RGS. Our RGS spectral analysis gives a three-dimensional Mach number of $0.48^{+0.22}_{-0.14}$, consistent with the power-spectrum results from Chandra for the same extraction region, and corresponding to a turbulent-to-thermal energy density ratio of $\sim0.13$. The warm-gas VSF follows the expectation for Kolmogorov turbulence and is broadly consistent with the hot-gas kinematics. The off-center warm gas in NGC 1404 may have formed through radiative cooling of the hot interstellar medium, triggered by the uplift of low-entropy hot gas during ram pressure stripping. Our study suggests that ram pressure stripping can drive substantial gas motions and reshape the thermodynamic state of the interstellar medium of cluster member galaxies.

2611.29772.abstract: Modelling multiphase gas in and around galaxies is key to understanding the baryon cycle in galaxy evolution. Modern simulation codes rely on heating/cooling functions and ion fractions to capture the thermodynamics and chemistry of such gases, but coupling all physical factors remains challenging. We present a new Python-based, parallelised package that acts as an integration framework, connecting well-established astrophysical codes and models to produce self-consistent heating/cooling functions and ion fractions from custom ionising UV/X-ray backgrounds. The package returns multi-dimensional tables that can be readily coupled to hydrodynamic and post-processing codes to study radiative processes and extract observables, as we demonstrate with static cloud simulations. Our simulation suite studies the thermodynamic history of a static circumgalactic cloud with smoothed edges subjected to meta-galactic and starburst heating. We find that the clouds experience damped pulsations regulated by strong cooling-driven inflows and heating-driven outflows that constantly overshoot pressure equilibrium. Meta-galactic heating is weak and produces a confined and dense cloud, while starburst heating is strong and sustains large clouds only a little smaller than those obtained with the standard $10^4\,\rm K$ cooling floor. Starburst radiative heating acts as a damping agent, thereby reducing mixing. py4radiation comes with extensive documentation and a sample catalogue of heating/cooling functions and ion tables for a selected set of input meta-galactic and starburst spectral energy distributions. The code is publicly available and can be easily expanded.

2611.29794.abstract: We present the first analysis of the Sutlej stellar stream using deep DECam photometry from the third data release of the DECam Local Volume Exploration Survey (DELVE DR3). Sutlej was discovered in Gaia DR3 as two parallel branches of old, metal-poor stars in projection near the SMC. Our DELVE DR3 sample reaches $\sim$2.5-3.5 mag below the main-sequence turnoff of Sutlej, and with a main-sequence matched filter built from an isochrone fit to Sutlej, we recover both previously identified branches, and find additional structure between them and at the periphery of the stream, occupying a region of $\sim$11$^\circ$ $\times$ 7$^\circ$ scattered at $\sim$23-33 kpc. We investigate this region by separating it into four segments that have Sutlej-like properties. The isochrone is also consistent with the nearby ultra-faint satellite Tucana III (Tuc III), and the two systems have similar distances and proper motions. $N$-body simulations of a Tuc III-like satellite show that, once the passage of a massive LMC is accounted for, Tuc III's preceding pericentric passage was deep enough to strip most of the progenitor. The encounter with the LMC then spreads the debris across the Sutlej field at the observed distances and proper motions, though the models do not recreate the observed discrete overdensities. We find that Sutlej is compatible with a Tuc III origin.

2611.30054.abstract: Protoclusters, the progenitors of galaxy clusters, provide ideal laboratories for studying how high-density environments influence galaxy formation and evolution at early cosmic epochs. It remains unclear whether environmental effects on galaxy properties over scales of $>30$ cMpc are already in place at $z > 2$ and how these effects depend on the evolutionary stage of large-scale structures. We investigate the physical properties of H$\alpha$ emitters (HAEs) in two extremely overdense protoclusters, BOSS1244 and BOSS1542, at $z = 2.24$, and explore the environmental dependence of galaxy properties at this redshift. In BOSS1244, we find a clear color-density and stellar mass-density relation. HAEs in higher-density regions are significantly redder in $z_{\rm s}-K_{\rm s}$ and more massive than those in lower-density regions. In contrast, BOSS1542 shows weak or no such correlations. Red HAEs $(z_{\rm s}-K_{\rm s}>2.5)$ in both fields are preferentially located in the densest cores, have high stellar masses $(>10^{11}\,M_{\odot})$, high SFRs, and are $4-7$ times more abundant than in general fields. The irregular morphologies observed in some red HAEs are consistent with ongoing mass assembly and may be associated with dust-obscured star formation or galaxy interactions. Both protoclusters broadly follow the star-forming main sequence, but BOSS1542 exhibits a steeper slope, indicating more active star formation in massive galaxies. Our results demonstrate that environmental effects on galaxy properties operate over scales of $\sim39$\,cMpc at $z=2.24$, but their manifestation is strongly dependent on the evolutionary state of the large-scale structure. BOSS1244 appears more evolved, with ongoing galaxy merging and possible quenching, while BOSS1542 remains in an early, filamentary, gas-rich phase.

2611.30268.abstract: The enrichment of heavy elements in the interstellar medium is central to understanding galaxy evolution. Oxygen, the most abundant element after H and He, provides the principal tracer of gas-phase metallicity, typically measured using nebular emission lines in star-forming regions. However, a long-standing issue-the abundance discrepancy factor (ADF)-produces a $\sim 0.25$ dex offset between metallicities derived from recombination lines (RLs) and collisionally excited lines (CELs). We present deep spectroscopic observations of the Orion Nebula (M42), and use them to assess the contribution of the often neglected continuum pumping process. We find that the continuum pumping effect is at least a factor of two stronger than previously expected. After accounting for the flux contribution from continuum pumping, the RL metallicity is consistent with the CEL metallicity, thus explaining the bulk of the ADF. Reassessing O/H measurements in five literature star-forming regions using the same method, we similarly find a systematic reduction of RL-based metallicities. These results indicate that RL metallicities, which have previously been considered more reliable than CELs, are subject to potentially large bias from continuum pumping. This study provides a foundation to correct this bias and establish accurate element abundance scales throughout cosmic time.

2611.30270.abstract: The oxygen abundance of H II regions is a fundamental tracer of chemical enrichment and gas cycling and is now routinely measured across a broad range of cosmic time. A persistent complication is the abundance discrepancy factor (ADF): the O$^{++}$/H$^+$ abundance inferred from optical recombination lines (RLs) is systematically higher than that inferred from collisionally excited lines (CELs). Small-scale temperature fluctuations within the O$^{++}$-emitting gas are among the most widely discussed explanations for this discrepancy. However, the recent identification of a substantial continuum-pumping contribution to the O II spectrum of M42 motivates a renewed assessment of which observations uniquely favor a temperature-based interpretation and which are also compatible with other mechanisms. In this first paper of a series, I examine the relation between the inferred temperature-fluctuation parameter, $t^2$, and interionic temperature differences, focusing on $\Delta T_e=T_e([OIII])-T_e([NII])$. Photoionization calculations show that ionization stratification naturally produces systematic temperature differences between the low- and high-ionization zones. Meanwhile, the conversion from an ADF to $t^2$ is strongly temperature dependent because CEL emissivities are nonlinear functions of electron temperature. I show that these two effects can account for much of the observed $t^2$-$\Delta T_e$ relation without requiring the interionic temperature difference itself to trace fluctuations within the O$^{++}$ zone. This result does not exclude temperature fluctuations in H II regions. Instead, it indicates that interionic temperature differences should be interpreted with care and, on their own, provide limited discrimination among proposed origins of the ADF.

2611.30357.abstract: We present a blind search for Galactic OH 18-cm absorption lines towards 19,130 radio sources brighter than 1mJy at 1.4GHz, using 390 pointings of the MeerKAT Absorption Line Survey (MALS). We apply an automated line search followed by Bayesian nested sampling to identify OH 1667MHz, 1665MHz and 1612MHz absorption features, using HI emission and absorption profiles as physically motivated priors. We identify 15 confident detections of OH 1667/1665 MHz absorption. The majority of detections are associated with a visual extinction ($A_{\rm V}$) excess and, within the same MALS pointings, with detected CO emission and a high incidence rate of HI absorption, consistent with OH tracing the H$_2$-bearing medium. We also identify 9 candidates of OH 1612MHz satellite line absorption, two of which coincide with OH main line detections and show integrated optical depth ratios well above the LTE expectation of 1:9. As in previous studies, $N(\rm OH)$ shows no dependence on $N$(HI). Accounting for the varying sensitivity across sight lines, we estimate the covering fraction of OH-bearing gas at $\log N(\rm OH) > 12$ to be $C = 0.051 \pm 0.008$, providing an independent and a more precise estimate than previous measurements of the diffuse molecular gas. We also find qualitative evidence for a decrease of the covering fraction with Galactic latitude. Stacking reveals a clear OH absorption signal that becomes increasingly prominent when sight lines are weighted by $A_{\rm V}$ excess, independently confirming the association of OH with diffuse molecular gas. Modeling of the physical conditions yields hydrogen number densities of 10-100 cm$^{-3}$, typical H$_2$ column densities $\log N(\rm H_2) > 21$, and UV-flux to number density ratios of 0.01-0.3 Mathis cm$^{3}$, typical of the CNM.

2611.30384.abstract: We present deep X-shooter follow-up spectroscopy of AMORE6, an exceptionally metal-poor galaxy at z = 5.725. The new spectrum provides stringent upper limits on rest-frame ultraviolet metal lines, including NV, CIV, NIV], NIII], and OIII]. The non-detection of CIV breaks the density-metallicity degeneracy present in previous analyses based on the [OIII]/Hbeta ratio, excluding the high-density, chemically enriched gas scenario and strengthening the evidence for an extremely metal-poor environment. The X-shooter spectrum also reveals a narrow Lyman-alpha line with a velocity dispersion sigma_v = 23.2 +/- 0.5 km/s and a nearly symmetric profile centered at the systemic redshift measured from Hbeta. Combining the Lyman-alpha line width with the measured source size, we infer a dynamical mass M_dyn = (1-22) x 10^7 Msun, assuming that the line width traces gravitational motions. Spectral energy distribution modeling using Pop III and Pop II stellar population libraries yields stellar masses (1-5) x 10^5 Msun. Although all models reproduce the observed blue UV continuum and Halpha equivalent width (EW), none simultaneously reproduces the Hbeta luminosity and EW, with the observed Hbeta luminosity exceeding the model predictions by up to 3.7 sigma. Possible explanations include departures from standard recombination conditions or limitations in the adopted stellar population models. We discuss possible interpretations of AMORE6, including massive-star formation in an atomic-cooling halo and a gravitationally bound star cluster.

2611.30457.abstract: Pairs of galaxies in which both objects host kiloparsec-scale radio jets are extremely rare. Such systems provide unique opportunity to study the formation of relativistic jets and their resistance to side-way collisions with each other prior to their eventual merger. We analyse the radio data for the twin radio galaxy J104455+354055 associated with a pair of distant elliptical galaxies (z=0.163). The radio jets of both sources avoid disruption/merging for the initial tens of kiloparsecs. We investigate the role of the magnetic fields in the propagation of these radio jets. We used VLA radio data at high frequencies in both compact and extended array configurations to obtain sensitive high-resolution polarimetric data and study the properties of the magnetic fields in all jets. Polarisation data suggest shearing of the magnetic fields at points where the jets bend. The orientation of the magnetic field parallel to jet axis helps confine the jet. Such field configuration in two adjacent jets seems to prevent them from merging. The strength of the magnetic field slightly increases in jet bends and the associated shearing enhances the ordered component of the magnetic field. The more diffuse radio plumes at the end of each jet have comparable strengths and energies of the magnetic field. The twin radio galaxy J104455+354055 provides a unique possibility to study the interplay of radio jets of two radio galaxies. The analysis of the properties of the magnetic fields observed along the radio jets suggests that the wiggles and bends of these jets, caused by the likely interactions of the host galaxies, could be also governed by the magnetic fields that may prevent them from merging. The derived strengths and energies of the magnetic field in different parts of the jets should allow us to improve the magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations of radio galaxies.

2611.30668.abstract: AIMS: By combining CH3CCH and CCH, we present a first multi-transition analysis of the RCW122-NE and RCW122-SW regions in the massive star-forming complex RCW 122. The aim is to investigate and to constrain the nature, chemistry, and evolutionary stage of each region. METHODS: We performed observations with the Atacama Pathfinder Experiment (APEX). The analysis is based on 39 CH3CCH lines with J=10-9 to 20-19 (170.8-341.8 GHz) and four hyperfine components of the CCH N=4-3 transition (349.1-349.6 GHz). We estimated excitation conditions using both local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) and non-LTE methods, with rotational-diagram analysis and Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) calculations. Gas-grain chemical models were performed with the Nautilus code to reproduce the observed abundances over timescales characteristic of high-mass YSO evolution. RESULTS: The excitation analysis of CH3CCH indicates two physical components suggestive of a thermal gradient. The NE region yields T~41-61 K and N_tot~1x10^{16} cm^{-2}, while SW exhibits T~33-48 K and N_tot~7x10^{15} cm^{-2}. In both regions, CCH traces cold gas below 15 K with an H_2 density of 0.5-4x10^6 cm^{-3}. The detection of the ^{13}C isotopologues of CCH indicates that C^{13}CH is more abundant than ^{13}CCH. Chemical models at various evolutionary stages, with cosmic rays as a key parameter, reproduce the observed CCH and CH3CCH abundances, although the two species form through chemically distinct routes. CONCLUSIONS: We provide a coherent scenario in which CCH traces colder gas at an early evolutionary stage, whereas CH3CCH traces a region characterized by a warmer temperature gradient, associated with chemically more evolved gas at a later stage. These results constrain the conditions governing the origin and survival of interstellar species in a thermally and chemically stratified medium.

2611.30730.abstract: [ABRIDGED] Context: Whether the initial mass function (IMF) varies with environment remains a central question in star formation. The multiple populations of Orion OB1b provide an ideal laboratory to test possible IMF variations. Aims: We aim to characterise the stellar populations of Orion OB1b by identifying its constituent groups, assigning membership probabilities to individual sources, and determining their IMFs. Methods: Using Gaia DR3 astrometry and photometry, we identified stellar groups through clustering analysis and assigned membership probabilities with a probabilistic mixture model. Stellar masses were derived from extinction-corrected photometry using pre-main-sequence evolutionary models. Results: We identified eight kinematically distinct groups and a non-clustered population, deriving ages and IMFs spanning ${\sim}0.08$--$10\,M_\odot$ for six groups, all consistent with being gravitationally unbound. Each IMF was fitted with a lognormal distribution below $1M_\odot$ and a power law above. The high-mass regime is statistically indistinguishable across all groups, while four groups also exhibit consistent IMFs over the full mass range. The remaining two groups show differences that may reflect membership uncertainties rather than intrinsic IMF variations. The combined IMF is characterised by $m_c=0.27^{+0.02}_{-0.02},M_\odot$, $\sigma=0.45^{+0.03}_{-0.03}$, and $\Gamma=1.85^{+0.16}_{-0.14}$. The non-clustered population exhibits a broader and more uncertain IMF, although residual field contamination cannot be ruled out. Conclusions: Our results support previous evidence for the complex internal structure of OB1b. The IMF in OB1b appears broadly consistent across its kinematically distinct groups and compatible with other young populations in Orion.

2611.30872.abstract: Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) will observe millions of galactic binaries (GBs) at once, thousands of them resolvable, with signals that overlap in frequency. Separating them requires a global fit, a joint inference of all sources, which today takes Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) samplers hours to days on a cluster and is repeated for each new stretch of data. We adapt recent advances in large-scale diffusion models, flow matching with a multimodal transformer, to learn the joint posterior once and then draw from it in a fraction of a second. We evaluate our approach on a realistic simulator, with full instrument response and noise, priors fitted to a simulated Galactic catalogue, and sources sampled anywhere in the entire 0.1 to 16 mHz frequency band. We demonstrate that the approach is scalable to up to 15 653 sources fitted simultaneously, evaluating calibration and coverage w.r.t. the MCMC baseline. The results show that this approach could be realistically scaled to tackle the full global fit problem.

2611.30991.abstract: We use the POSSUM catalog with its high density of background RM sources (30-50 per square degree) to extend previous LOFAR work and investigate the sign of galactic halo magnetic fields. We are searching for the universal configuration that arises if halo magnetization originates from a central Cosmic Battery, and is subsequently transported outward by large-scale outflows. Our analysis considers 10 edge-on galaxies in the field of view of the POSSUM survey with angular sizes between 60 and 100. For each such galaxy we collect all available background RM sources in a circular region with a radius of 2? around it. We rescale all galaxy sizes and their associated background RM source distances to a common galaxy size of 100 and stack all these regions together. We divide the stacked configuration of RM sources into the four quadrants on either side of the stacked galaxy axis. The mean RM of background sources is computed in each quadrant, and we obtain a pattern of positive and negative mean RM values around the stacked galaxy. A consistent, systematic RM-gradient pattern emerges inside about 6 stacked galactic radii, as expected in Magnetic Disk-Winds with the axial magnetic field configuration predicted by the Cosmic Battery. The inferred large-scale axial electric current in the halo flows from the center outwards. Beyond 6 galactic radii we observe the reverse mean RM pattern, as expected in the axial Magnetic Black-Hole Jet configuration predicted by the Cosmic Battery. Our work confirms the prediction of the Cosmic Battery, and presents one of the very few known signatures of the magnetic field in the halo and the circumgalactic medium (CGM).

2611.31148.abstract: JWST observations have revealed a higher-than-expected abundance of bright galaxies at $z \gtrsim 10$. Several scenarios have been proposed to explain this excess, one of which invokes a top-heavy stellar initial mass function (IMF) in the early Universe. In this work, we construct spectral energy distribution (SED) templates based on a redshift- and metallicity-dependent IMF ($z$-$Z$ dependent IMF) motivated by the star-cluster simulations of Chon et al. (2022) and the redshift-dependent IMF model of Steinhardt et al. (2020). We implement these templates in a semi-analytic galaxy model built on a large-box $N$-body simulation to investigate the impact of a top-heavy IMF on the ultraviolet luminosity function (UVLF) of high-redshift galaxies. The adopted $z$-$Z$ dependent IMF enhances the UV luminosity of young stellar populations, particularly at low metallicity, and increases the scatter in the UV luminosity-to-star formation rate conversion factor relative to the Kroupa IMF. Without dust attenuation, both top-heavy IMF models predict a substantially enhanced bright end of the UVLF. However, when dust attenuation is included and calibrated at $z=7$, IMF-dependent metal enrichment and the resulting dust attenuation partly offset the intrinsic UV enhancement. The self-consistent model broadly reproduces the observed UVLF at $z\sim10$, although discrepancies remain at $z\gtrsim12$. For the selected high-redshift UVLF constraints, the best-fitting dust optical depths are 51% and 21% of the fiducial values at $z=9.7$ and $13.04$, respectively, indicating a preference for weaker effective dust attenuation. The highest-redshift comparison does not provide a robust constraint. Our results highlight the importance of accounting for both enhanced stellar UV emission and IMF-dependent metal enrichment and dust attenuation when assessing the impact of a top-heavy IMF on high-redshift galaxies.

2611.31231.abstract: The Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1) strong lens search presents ECLIPSE, the largest catalogue of strong gravitational lens candidates to date, with >15 000 systems identified across 1900 deg2 of sky. It was constructed using five neural networks applied to approximately 68 million galaxies, followed by citizen science and expert visual inspection. In this work, we compare how the independently developed networks use image information to identify their selection of strong lens candidates. The search combines convolutional neural networks and a vision transformer, using the same pool of data but with different image processing and training choices. We investigate why these networks find different systems and what that means for the completeness of our catalogue. We evaluate all networks on a 50 deg2 calibration set and their application to the full DR1 sample. We find that the networks score candidates very differently, and that combining them recovers over 500 lens candidates within our calibration set at an inspection budget of 2000 objects. On the full DR1 sample, we show that individual networks have distinct biases: some networks favour systems with a larger Einstein radius while others are more sensitive to compact configurations. We also investigate network preferences in terms of lens light profile, mass distribution geometry, photometric redshift, and magnitudes. These findings provide a detailed analysis of how neural network selection biases have shaped the Euclid DR1 ECLIPSE catalogue. The results inform how networks should be combined in future Euclid data releases and upcoming wide-field surveys such as LSST or Roman to maximise both completeness and diversity of the recovered lens population.

2611.28334.abstract: We present a study that simultaneously fits for key fast radio burst (FRB) population properties using the Second CHIME/FRB Catalog while calibrating for instrumental selection effects. Our inferred volumetric rate at $z=0$ is $1.1^{+0.4}_{-0.3}\times 10^{5}\,{\rm Gpc}^{-3}\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$ above an isotropic-equivalent energy of $10^{39}$ erg and below a scattering timescale of 30 ms at 600 MHz. The evolution of the FRB rate relative to the cosmic star formation rate remains statistically unconstrained. Assuming a Schechter function for the energy distribution, isotropic emission, and 1-GHz emission bandwidth, we find a characteristic maximum energy of $2.0^{+2.6}_{-1.0} \times 10^{41}$ erg and a differential power-law index of $-1.41\,^{+0.27}_{-0.21}({\rm stat.})\,\pm\,0.35({\rm sys.})$. The host galaxy contribution to the observed dispersion measure (DM) is modeled as a log-normal distribution; assuming a total Galactic contribution of 80 $\text{pc cm}^{-3}$, we find a median host-galaxy DM contribution of $199^{+34}_{-36}\;\text{pc cm}^{-3}$ in the rest-frame. Finally, we find that the average FRB spectrum, described by a spectral index of $\alpha=-1.0^{+0.5}_{-0.6}$, is inconsistent with being flat at the $\sim2\sigma$ level. We note an excess of high-S/N bursts at low DMs in the observed sample that is not predicted by the best-fit model. Testing alternative models does not alleviate this tension; future population studies may mitigate this limitation by incorporating robust fluence and redshift measurements.

2611.28537.abstract: Most stars in the field are part of binary, triple, or higher-order systems, which we primarily observe in hierarchical configurations that allow long-term stability. Over long timescales, hierarchical triple systems interact primarily through gravitational dynamics, but more complex interactions arise when stellar evolution drives mass transfer. In this paper, we study tertiary mass transfer in hierarchical triple systems using three-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations. We find that the finite separation of the inner binary produces oscillations in the Roche potential that critically alter both the donor star's variability and its mean mass-loss rate. For compact inner binaries, the mass-loss rate approaches that of a single accretor, while at larger separations the orbit-averaged mass-loss rate increases steeply, approximately as $\langle \dot{M}_d\rangle \propto \langle \dot{M}_{d,0}\rangle (1+C a_b^{6.1 \pm 0.9})$. For the $\gamma = 5/3$ polytropic donor considered here, this scaling is consistent with the nonlinear response of Roche-lobe overflow to the leading quadrupolar perturbation of the inner-binary potential, which scales as $\delta\Phi_2 \propto a_b^2$. We also examine the donor's response to periodic forcing from the inner binary and find a transition between individual and collaborative accretion that determines whether the transferred material can form and sustain a circumbinary disk. Our results show that the finite separation of the inner binary can strongly regulate both the rate and fate of tertiary mass transfer, constraining a poorly understood phase of hierarchical triple evolution.

2611.28969.abstract: We validate a subset of the astrometric accelerations reported in Gaia DR3 non-single-star solutions by their consistency with the gravitational pull of known, resolved companions. Cross-matching 338,215 DR3 acceleration solutions against the Washington Double Star (WDS) catalog of visual binaries yields 2,466 unique pairs within 2". For each pair we compare the measured acceleration with alpha_max, the Newtonian bound on the acceleration the companion can impart on the Gaia-tracked photocenter. For 98.1% of the pairs the measured acceleration exceeds this bound by more than a factor of 10, so the cataloged companion cannot be responsible and the perturber must be a closer, unresolved one. The remaining 45 plausible wide binaries are close pairs at the WDS resolution limit. We fit orbits with an updated orvara, extended to accept the DR3 acceleration and jerk coefficients as direct constraints and released with htof as part of this work. The fits converge for 16 of the 45 and one boundary case, the rest having too few resolved measures or a perturber other than the cataloged pair, and 13 of the 17 carry enough data to test the coefficients. Eleven of the 13 statistically accommodate the reported accelerations, for seven- and nine-parameter solutions alike, and the dynamical companion masses agree with the photometric estimates where the photocenter conversion is well determined. Independently of the fits, 33 of the 43 plausible systems with a usable position angle (77%) have the acceleration directed within 45 degrees of the primary-companion axis, against 50% for a control sample: DR3's measured accelerations point in the directions of the cataloged companions.

2611.29474.abstract: Some protostars undergo episodic accretion, resulting in luminosity outbursts that heat their envelopes. The increase in temperature alters the position of the snowlines, which return to their original locations on different timescales depending on the species. However, the chemical effects of luminosity outbursts in protostellar envelopes, including their long-term consequences, remain poorly explored. We investigate the chemical impact of luminosity outbursts on the envelope of a solar-type protostar, accounting for its dynamics, and identify trends in the molecular response relative to both ongoing and past outburst activity. We combined the dynamic semi-analytic code APE with the three-phase chemical model NAUTILUS to predict the time evolution of 83 molecular abundances between 10 and 10,000 au in the collapsing envelope. The outburst was parameterized by increasing the protostellar luminosity by a factor of 100 for 100 years. The outburst shifts molecular snowlines outward by up to a factor of ten, thus enriching the gas phase through thermal desorption. Most species return to their pre-outburst state within a few thousand years at most for r$\leq$1000 au and remain in that state thereafter. However, eight molecules (HOCH2CHO, CH3COCH2OH, C2H5CHO, OCS, SO2, C2S, C3S, and HC3N) show abundance deviations 10$-$50 kyr after the outburst in the warm inner regions (T$\geq$100 K), due to the inward transport of chemically altered material. Eight other species (CH3O, C2O, NH2, HCCO, HCNO, HNO, NO, and NCO) show enhanced gas-phase abundances at intermediate radii ($\sim$300$-$1500 au). Overall, most molecules are impacted by outward snowline shifts. With the exception of HOCH2CHO, CH3COCH2OH, and C2H5CHO, all complex organic molecules (COMs) are expected to exhibit similar abundances in the warm inner regions of protostars (hot corino), regardless of whether they undergo outbursts.
